body.text: Greens senator Mehreen Faruqi says she is disappointed by the result of the party's leadership ballot, following the election of David Shoebridge as leader.
Earlier, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese flagged the mid-year budget update in December would include measures to tackle the cost of living.

Full story: Shoebridge named new Greens leader in ballot
Just joining us and need a refresher on the latest with the Greens leadership ballot?
A friend of the blog, Erin Handley, has you covered.
Focus on One Nation not us, Chalmers tells new Greens leaders
Just before he wrapped up his press conference, Treasurer Jim Chalmers gave his two cents on the Greens leadership.
NSW senator David Shoebridge was elected to take over from Larissa Waters, who stepped down due to illness after 16 months in the job. Victorian Steph Hodgins-May will be his deputy.
Chalmers wished Waters well, saying he was sad to hear she's been unwell. "Larissa seems to me to be a wonderful person," he says.
He says he hasn't met the new leadership team but says Labor will continue to engage in "good faith" when it comes to negotiations in the Senate, where the government does not have the numbers.
The treasurer urged the new leadership team to keep their focus on One Nation after Shoebridge used his first remarks in the top job to take aim at Labor.
"I think it's really important that we focus on the risks posed to workers and to our economy by One Nation, the Liberal Party and the National Party," he says.
Chalmers on the defensive on productivity
Jim Chalmers has defended his track record after the RBA boss bluntly declared productivity was "doing nothing" to tackle persistent inflation.
The treasurer says the government made productivity the "central feature" of the May budget and acknowledged the challenge it posed.

"It will take a bit of time to turn it around because if there was an easy solution, an immediate solution, to the productivity challenge we see here in Australia and in most comparable countries, somebody would have done that already," he says.
Chalmers rebuffs criticism from former RBA boss
Treasurer Jim Chalmers has brushed off criticism from former RBA boss Philip Lowe, who called for the government to cut spending to take pressure off inflation.

Lowe told the Institute of Public Affairs podcast The Prosperity Question that government spending had been adding to demand, and Labor should be running surpluses instead given the low unemployment rate and high commodity prices.
The treasurer said Lowe was entitled to his view.
"He expresses it relatively regularly. My focus is on the job at hand, not on the commentary whether it's on the Institute of Public Affairs podcast or in other places," he said.

"My focus is on continuing to provide the responsible economic management that is necessary, in uncertain global conditions. That includes rolling out cost-of-living relief, cutting taxes, finding savings in an ongoing way."
Is Chalmers at odds with RBA governor? He doesn't think so
That's the question put to the treasurer after Michele Bullock said inflation was also being "driven by domestic capacity pressures".

Jim Chalmers doesn't agree with the characterisation. He says his argument that the inflation challenge was being made worse by the Middle East war was "entirely consistent" with the RBA board statement.
"I have acknowledged for some time that the inflation challenge in our economy has a number of factors associated with it," he says.
Chalmers says he confers and shares notes with Bullock regularly.
"I like working with her. We have similar objectives ... but we have different responsibilities."
Key Event
Fuel, wind back of energy rebates, Middle East war to blame for higher inflation: Chalmers
While all of that was going on, Treasurer Jim Chalmers held a press conference on the latest inflation figures.
Headline inflation jumped to 4 per cent last month on the back of higher fuel prices. Underlying inflation held steady at 3.6 per cent.
"These numbers confirm that the overwhelming reason why inflation went up in August in headline terms was higher global oil prices," Chalmers says.
"In fact, all of the increase in annual headline inflation was from a combination of higher fuel costs and the unwinding of last year's energy rebates."
But he concedes inflation remains too high.

"We already had an inflation challenge in our economy, but the war in the Middle East is making it worse, and that's why, from an economic point of view, the war in the Middle East can't end soon enough."
Key Event
Faruqi 'disappointed' by leadership ballot, calls for member vote
Mehreen Faruqi has released a statement after her failed bid for the Greens leadership.
The senator, who put her hat in the ring on a joint ticket alongside Nick McKim, said she was disappointed the party room did not back her in the ballot.
"Of course, I am disappointed the party room chose another direction, and know many others will feel the same way," she wrote.
Prior to today's vote, Faruqi was co-deputy leader. She did not recontest that position today.
"I did not stand for deputy leader today because, on reflection, I believe I can best play my part in that action outside the constraints of the leadership team," she said.
Faruqi says she was also frustrated that the leadership was not elected by Greens members.
"Without a member vote, we cannot call ourselves a grassroots party. I call on the new leadership team to set a timeline for a one member, one vote."
Opening party leader vote to members part of 'ongoing conversation': Shoebridge
David Shoebridge has been asked about a proposal by former Greens MP Max Chandler-Mather to allow party members to vote for the leader.
The new Greens leader says building a mass movement means connecting with the party membership.
He says he was elected on the rules governing the party today, but says opening up the vote is part of an "ongoing conversation" with members.

"We got elected today on the rules that have been set and we will be working with members across the country to create further democratisation of the party, to make people be part of a movement where they get to choose their elected representatives," he says.
Key Event
Greens will support 'material change' from Labor: Shoebridge
New Greens leader David Shoebridge says his party won't obstruct "material change" put on the table by Labor in parliament.
Labor relies on either the Coalition or the Greens to pass legislation through the Senate because it doesn't have a majority in the upper house.
Shoebridge says Labor presents "meaningless huffs and puffs" policies.

"I'll say this to the Labour Party: if you put serious material change on the on the table of the parliament, we'll vote for that," he says. "We're not here to make Labor better. They're proving that's not a project. That's why we need to replace Labor."
"I'll say this to the Labour Party: if you put serious material change on the on the table of the parliament, we'll vote for that," he says.
"We're not here to make Labor better. They're proving that's not a project. That's why we need to replace Labor."
Greens won't leave 'endless vacuum of nothingness' by Labor: Shoebridge
The new Greens leader says the party needs to bridge the gap with voters with a sense of political momentum and positivity.
David Shoebridge says the party has discussed initiatives about its strengths. He says the party is ready to "get out and make this fight".
"This is a challenge we're up to," Shoebridge says.
"What's the alternative to leave this kind of ... endless vacuum of nothingness delivered by the ALP, which only feeds One Nation? We will not let that happen."
Greens need to connect with voters who are angry with politics, Shoebridge says
David Shoebridge says the Australian Greens need to connect with millions of Australians who have legitimate anger with politics.
The new Greens leader says the party needs to convince Australians not to believe in the politics of "hate and division and fear".
"I hope we can come together to actually make jobs and opportunity for each other. This is the message we're giving, but it starts with recognising and feeling that," Shoebridge says.
Shoebridge urges media to listen to voices from progressive Jewish community
New Greens leader David Shoebridge says people are desperate for material change and don't want "meaningless messages" from Labor.
Asked how he will repair the party's relationship with the Jewish community, Shoebridge says the Greens have strong connections with people "fighting genocide".

"We will continue to champion their voices to be solid allies with them and I'd ask those in the media who are covering this issue to actually listen to these powerful principal voices coming from the progressive Jewish Australian community," he says.
Why haven't the Greens been able to capitalise on anti-major party sentiment?
Moving to questions, David Shoebridge has been asked why the Greens haven't been able to capitalise on the rise of anti-major party sentiment.
The new Greens leader says it's no wonder people are losing faith in politics as people struggle to pay their mortgages.

"What we are going to do collectively as the Greens is fill the policy vacuum that's been left by the Labor Party, explain to people, make the connections between what they're feeling as they can't afford to buy their groceries, or they're worried about the next bill that's coming down the line," Shoebridge says.
Hodgins-May says Greens want to bring 'bold vision' to Australia
Deputy Greens leader Steph Hodgins-May has stepped up to speak and used the opportunity to attack the federal government.
She's echoed comments from her leader, David Shoebridge, that the Greens want to replace Labor.
"We have a government that is letting corporations write the rules in this country, and the same goes for the opposition and One Nation," she says.

"Well, the Greens are not here to reform the Labor Party. We are here to replace the Labor Party. "I am looking forward to working with David to bring a bold vision to Australia, to grow our movement, to confront the impending climate crisis that is here now."
"Well, the Greens are not here to reform the Labor Party. We are here to replace the Labor Party.
"I am looking forward to working with David to bring a bold vision to Australia, to grow our movement, to confront the impending climate crisis that is here now."
Shoebridge says Greens want to replace Labor
David Shoebridge has pivoted to the priorities he'll tackle as Greens leader. He says families are anxious and concerned about affordability.
The new Greens leader says people are making decisions about whether to pay for insurance or pay for groceries.
He says the Greens do not exist to make the Labor Party better but rather to replace Labor.

"We present this fresh, new, strong face to build on the amazing work of Larissa and the team. But to make that connection between people's material lives, the struggles, the stresses, their pay and the failure of politics to meet the moment," Shoebridge says.
Shoebridge thanks Larissa Waters for leadership
New Greens leader David Shoebridge is talking now, and he's started by thanking Larissa Waters for taking on the leadership of the party.
Shoebridge says Waters rose to the occasion and led with compassion and principle, and "showed what collective leadership can do".
"Larissa had the rock solid and still has the love of the Australian Greens and so I want to thank Larissa for the leadership," Shoebridge says.
Waters says it was an 'incredible honour' to lead Greens
Former Greens Leader Larissa Waters is speaking now, and she says it has been an "incredible honour" to be leader of the Greens following the last election.
Waters says she was not able to continue in her role because of her chronic kidney condition, which has been getting worse.
"I'm really proud of how the team has worked together over the last 16 months, and I'm proud that our party is polling higher than ever before," Waters says.
"I'm proud of the time that I have spent leading this incredible team, I'm very proud to be a humble backbencher and a senator for Queensland after I take some medical leave."
David Shoebridge confirmed as Greens leader, Hodgins-May as deputy
The Greens have confirmed that NSW senator David Shoebridge has been elected party leader, with Victorian senator Steph Hodgins-May as deputy, in a ballot.
Greens whip Nick McKim says Shoebridge, NSW senator Mehreen Faruqi and SA senator Sarah Hanson-Young nominated for the leadership.
The vote came down to Shoebridge and Faruqi in the end with 7 votes to 4. Hanson-Young was eliminated in the first round of voting, only receiving two votes.
Hodgins-May, WA senator Jordan Steele-John and Tasmanian senator Vanessa Bleyer nominated for the deputy leadership, according to McKim.
Steph Hodgins-May elected as Greens deputy leader
A statement from the Greens has just dropped in our inboxes, confirming the joint ticket of David Shoebridge and Steph Hodgins-May has prevailed in today's leadership ballot.
"Labor has proven they can't stop One Nation because they made the conditions for them to thrive. The Greens can," Shoebridge said.
"Between us, Steph and I have taken on AUKUS, gas companies, lobbyists, billionaire AI companies, and the Labor government."
Key Event
Breaking: David Shoebridge chosen as Greens leader
NSW Greens senator David Shoebridge has been chosen as leader of the Australian Greens at a meeting of the party in Sydney.
Shoebridge defeated SA senator Sarah Hanson-Young and NSW senator Mehreen Faruqi for the leadership.
Shoebridge ran on a joint ticket with Victorian senator Steph Hodgins-May.
We expect more details at a press conference due to be held in a few minutes, including who will be the party's deputy.
